title: Finite-index free lattice enlargement through a divisible subgroup
statement: Let $n\geq1$ be an integer, let $L$ be a free abelian group of finite rank (a finite free $\mathbf Z$-module [def-weil-pbc-free-module]), let $B$ be an abelian group, let $D\subset B$ be a subgroup, and let $\varphi:L\to B$ be a group homomorphism. Suppose $D$ is $n$-divisible (for every $d\in D$ there is $e\in D$ with $ne=d$), $B/D$ is torsion-free (multiplication by every positive integer is injective), and $(B/D)/\operatorname{im}(L)$ is finite and killed by $n$. Then there exist a free abelian group $G$ of finite rank, an injective homomorphism $i:L\to G$ with $G/i(L)$ killed by a power of $n$, and a homomorphism $h:G\to B$ with $h\circ i=\varphi$, such that $G\to B/D$ is surjective. Free of finite rank means isomorphic to $\mathbf Z^d$ for some finite $d\geq0$.

proof.text: Write $C=B/D$, let $p:B\to C$ be the quotient map, put $f=p\varphi$, and put $Q=C/f(L)$. Prove the assertion by strong induction on the positive integer $|Q|$, keeping $n,B,D$ fixed and allowing $L,\varphi$ to vary. If $|Q|=1$, take $G=L$, $i=\operatorname{id}$ and $h=\varphi$. The quotient $G/i(L)=0$ is killed by $n^0=1$, and $ph=f$ is surjective.

source.place: Expose XVI, Lemma 3.6.4 and proof, printed pp.252--253; explicit cyclic pushout and induction.

proof.text: If $|Q|>1$, choose a nonzero class $q\in Q$, represented by $c\in C$, and choose $b\in B$ with $p(b)=c$. Let $d\geq2$ be the least positive integer with $dq=0$; it exists since $nq=0$. Euclidean division shows that $kq=0$ holds exactly when $d$ divides $k$, for every integer $k$: divide $k$ by $d$ and use minimality of $d$ on the remainder. In particular $d\mid n$. Choose $a\in L$ with $f(a)=dc$, and set $u=db-\varphi(a)\in D$.

source.place: Expose XVI, Lemma 3.6.4 and proof, printed pp.252--253; explicit cyclic pushout and induction.

proof.text: Write $n=de$ with $e\geq1$. By $n$-divisibility choose $v\in D$ with $nv=u$ and put $\widetilde u=ev$, so $d\widetilde u=u$. Replace $b$ by $b-\widetilde u$; its image remains $c$, and now $db=\varphi(a)$. Only divisibility by $n$, and consequently by its divisor $d$, has been used.

source.place: Expose XVI, Lemma 3.6.4 and proof, printed pp.252--253; explicit cyclic pushout and induction.

proof.text: The following explicit relation calculation will make the cyclic adjunction well defined. If $dx+ka=0$ in $L$, for $x\in L$ and $k\in\mathbf Z$, applying $f$ gives $d(f(x)+kc)=0$. Torsion-freeness of $C$ gives $f(x)+kc=0$, hence $kq=0$. By Step 2, $k=dt$ for some $t\in\mathbf Z$. The original equation becomes $d(x+ta)=0$, and $L$ is torsion-free since it has a free basis over $\mathbf Z$. Thus $x=-ta$. Conversely $(x,k)=(-ta,dt)$ satisfies $dx+ka=0$.

source.place: Expose XVI, Lemma 3.6.4 and proof, printed pp.252--253; explicit cyclic pushout and induction.

proof.text: Define the actual subgroup $L_1=dL+\mathbf Za=\{dx+ka:x\in L,\ k\in\mathbf Z\}\subset L$. Fix a finite basis identifying $L$ with $\mathbf Z^J$. The image of $L_1$ is a subgroup of $\mathbf Z^J$, so [lem-weil-subgroup-finite-free-abelian-group-free] says exactly that $L_1$ is free of finite rank. Define $j:L\to L_1$ by $j(x)=dx$. It is injective because $d\geq1$ and $L$ is torsion-free.

source.place: Expose XVI, Lemma 3.6.4 and proof, printed pp.252--253; explicit cyclic pushout and induction.

proof.text: Define $\varphi_1:L_1\to B$ by $\varphi_1(dx+ka)=\varphi(x)+kb$. This is independent of the presentation: by Step 4 the difference of two presentations is $(-ta,dt)$, whose proposed image is $-t\varphi(a)+tdb=0$ by Step 3. Adding presentations proves additivity, and $\varphi_1j=\varphi$. Moreover $L_1/j(L)$ is generated by the class of $a$, and $da=j(a)$, so it is killed by $d$ and hence by $n$.

source.place: Expose XVI, Lemma 3.6.4 and proof, printed pp.252--253; explicit cyclic pushout and induction.

proof.text: Put $f_1=p\varphi_1$. Directly from its formula, $f_1(L_1)=f(L)+\mathbf Zc$. The map $C\to Q/\langle q\rangle$ is surjective and has kernel $f(L)+\mathbf Zc$, giving a bijection $C/f_1(L_1)\simeq Q/\langle q\rangle$ by sending the class of $z$ to the class of its image in $Q$. The subgroup $\langle q\rangle$ has the $d$ distinct elements $0,q,\ldots,(d-1)q$; its cosets partition $Q$ into sets of size $d$. Thus the new cokernel is finite of cardinality $|Q|/d<|Q|$, and it is still killed by $n$ because it is a quotient of $Q$.

source.place: Expose XVI, Lemma 3.6.4 and proof, printed pp.252--253; explicit cyclic pushout and induction.

proof.text: Apply the induction hypothesis to $L_1,\varphi_1$ with the same $n,B,D$. Step 5 gives finite freeness, Step 7 gives the required smaller finite cokernel killed by $n$, and divisibility of $D$ and torsion-freeness of $C$ are unchanged. Obtain $i_1:L_1\hookrightarrow G$ and $h:G\to B$ with $hi_1=\varphi_1$, $ph$ surjective, and $n^sG\subset i_1(L_1)$ for some $s\geq0$. Set $i=i_1j$. It is injective and $hi=\varphi_1j=\varphi$. For $g\in G$, write $n^sg=i_1(y)$. Step 6 gives $ny\in j(L)$, whence $n^{s+1}g=i_1(ny)\in i(L)$. Thus $G/i(L)$ is killed by $n^{s+1}$, which proves every requested clause.
